blocks.text: The Final Unknown is the graduation exercise for this book. It is not a test of what you remember. It is a test of what you can do — under conditions this book has not shown you.

You will be given a scenario. You will not be told which framework to use. You will not be told what the right answer is. You will have to observe, define, ask, think, decide, act, adapt, and reflect — using whatever the previous eight Levels installed in you.
There is no answer key. The point is not what you decide. The point is how you decide, and what you learn from having decided.
**THE SCENARIO — Six weeks. One mandate. Incomplete information.**

You have just been appointed interim head of a struggling department at a company you joined nine months ago. Twelve people report to you. Your predecessor was fired last Friday in circumstances the CEO has described only as 'complicated.'
The CEO has given you a mandate: 'Fix this department in six weeks. I want a plan by day 14, visible progress by day 30, and results by day 42.'
What you know:
• Team morale is low. Two of the twelve are visibly disengaged. One is actively looking to leave.
• A key vendor relationship is at risk. The vendor sent an email last month asking for a call that your predecessor never returned.
• The team's biggest customer is unhappy about a delivery that missed its target eight weeks ago. The customer's point of contact has stopped responding to emails.
• There is a project underway that consumes 40% of the team's capacity. You do not yet understand whether it is important.
• Your predecessor's manager — the CEO — has a reputation for being impatient. Two other department heads were replaced in the last year.
What you do not know:
• Why your predecessor was actually fired.
• Which of the twelve are the ones worth keeping.
• What the CEO means by 'fix this department.'
• Whether the 40%-capacity project is important or a sunk-cost carousel.
• Which of your predecessor's decisions to preserve, and which to undo.
You have six weeks. You are being watched.
Do not read further until you have spent at least 30 minutes with the scenario. Write down what you would do — specifically, day by day, for the first two weeks.
Take it seriously. This is exactly the kind of situation the book was designed to prepare you for.
Below, we walk through what a capable person would do. There is no single correct answer. But there is a set of moves that consistently produce better outcomes than the alternatives.
Days 1–3: Do not fix anything yet

The single most common failure in this situation is trying to fix things before understanding them. The predecessor was fired. You do not know why. You do not know what is load-bearing and what is legacy.
Your first three days: observe. Interview all twelve individually. Not for 15 minutes each — for 45. Same four questions to everyone:

items: What is working well right now?
What is not working, and what should we do about it?
What does success look like from your seat?
What have you been reluctant to tell leadership until now?

blocks.text: Take notes. Do not commit to anything. Listen.
Days 4–7: Interview outward

Now the customer, the vendor, and your peers. Same listening posture. You are looking for pattern-matches across all these conversations. Where do three or more people independently mention the same problem? That is a real problem.

Also: schedule a 30-minute conversation with the CEO. One agenda: 'What does 'fix this department' actually mean to you? What does day 42 look like if we've succeeded?' You must know the target before you optimize.
Days 8–13: Define the actual problem

By now you should have enough data to distinguish surface problems from underlying ones. Almost certainly the 'problem' you were told to fix is a symptom of one or two underlying issues. Common patterns:

items: Broken trust with a key stakeholder that has cascaded into performance issues.
A misallocated project that is consuming capacity while producing little value.
A missing skill or role that would be much cheaper to fill than to work around.
A cultural pattern from the previous leader that everyone worked around but no one addressed.

blocks.text: Use the Level 2 problem-definition tool. Write out the 5-level problem statement. Bring it to the CEO on day 14 as the plan.
Day 14: The plan
What you present to the CEO on day 14 is NOT a conventional operational plan. It is:

items: A short paragraph on what you actually diagnosed as the underlying problem.
Three to five specific moves you propose to make.
The one move you would kill (a current initiative that isn't producing value).
The person you would hire or role you would create.
The specific metric that will indicate success on day 42, along with your honest probability estimate that it will improve.

blocks.text: Not a Gantt chart. A one-page thesis. Signed with your name. Owned.
Days 15–30: Execute the top move
Do not try to do all five moves at once. Pick the ONE with highest leverage. Execute it. Communicate the priority to your team so they know what to focus on.
Have the difficult conversations you've been avoiding (Level 4). Send the vendor the message your predecessor never sent. Fly to the customer if needed. Make the hiring decision.
Concurrently, kill the initiative you identified as waste. Do it publicly, with a clear reason. Killing a project cleanly earns more credibility than any launch.
Days 31–42: Measure and adapt
Check the metric. Adjust. Continue executing.
Also: begin the second move. Never try to run three moves in parallel until at least one has clearly worked.
Day 42: The debrief
Deliver to the CEO:

Honesty about the 'didn't work' section is what distinguishes senior operators from junior ones. The CEO already knows something didn't work. Your job is to show that YOU know it, and can explain why.
Not on a checklist. On the following (self-)questions:

rows: Self-control
Did you resist the urge to fix things on day 1? Did you stay calm when the CEO's impatience became visible?
Observation
Did you actually listen — or did you form a story in the first three interviews and confirm it in the next nine?
Critical thinking
Did you distinguish the surface problem from the underlying one? Did you notice what wasn't being said?
Resourcefulness
Did you find the information you needed — from customers, vendors, peers, HR? Or did you rely only on what your team told you?
Communication
Did you set expectations clearly with the CEO, the team, the customer? Did you communicate the difficult decisions with clarity?
People intelligence
Did you handle the disengaged team members with care? Did you have the vendor conversation with respect for what your predecessor may have done?
Execution
Did you pick a leverage move and execute? Or spread thin across five things?
Decision-making
Did you use a framework, or did you optimize for looking decisive? Are you clear on which of your day-14 decisions you would revisit?
Adaptability
When something on your plan didn't work, did you adjust — or defend?
Character
Did you tell the CEO the honest version, including the parts that make you look imperfect?

blocks.text: Score yourself honestly. Not against perfection. Against who you were nine months ago.
Regardless of the outcome — whether the CEO praises you, fires you, or promotes you — ask yourself:
*Would I be proud of how I handled this?*
If yes: this is the beginning of a career built on capability, not luck. Your reputation will compound in ways that a single outcome cannot.
If no: the specific way in which you fell short is the curriculum for your next six months. Own it. Fix it. Come back stronger.
Neither the promotion nor the firing is the measure. Your self-respect is the measure.
REMEMBER THIS
*“The Final Unknown is not a test of what you learned. It is a test of who you have become.”*
